edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), De poenitentia, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Hucusque, Christe Domine, de poenitentiae disciplina servis tuis dicere vel audire contingat, quousque etiam delinquere non oportet audientibus: vel nihil jam de poenitentia noverint, nihil ejus requirant. Piget fecundae, imo iam ultimae spei subtexere mentionem, ne retractantes de residuo auxilio poenitendi, spatium adhuc delinquendi demonstrare videamur. Absit, ut aliquis ita interpretetur, quasi eo sibi etiam nunc pateat ad delinquendum, quia patet ad poenitendum; et redundantia clementiae coelestis, libidinem faciat humanae temeritatis. Nemo idcirco deterior sit, quia Deus melior est, totiens delinquendo quotiens ignoscitur. Caeterum finem utique evadendi habebit. cum offendendi non habebit. Evasimus semel; hactenus periculosis nosmetipsos inferamus, et si iterum evasuri videmur. Plerique naufragio liberati exinde repudium et navi et mari dicunt, et Dei beneficium, salutem suam scilicet, memoria periculi honorant. Laudo timorem, diligo verecundiam, nolunt iterum divinae misericordiae oneri esse; formidant videri inculcare, quod consecuti sunt; bona certe sollicitudine iterum experiri vitant quod semel didicerunt timere. Ita modus temeritatis, testatio est timoris. Timor autem hominis, Dei honor est. Sed enim pervicacissimus hostis ille, nunquam malitiae suae otium facit. Atquin tunc maxime saevit, cum hominem plene sentit liberatum; tunc plurimum accenditur, dum extinguitur. Doleat et ingemiscat necesse est, venia peccatorum permissa, tot in homine mortis opera diruta, tot titulos damnationis retro suae erasos. Dolet quod ipsum et angelos ejus, Christi servus illi peccator judicaturus est. Itaque observat, oppugnat, obsidet, si qua possit aut oculos concupiscentia carnali ferire, aut animum illecebris saecularibus irretire, aut fidem terrenae potestatis formidine evertere, aut a via certa perversis traditionibus detorquere: non scandalis, non tentationibus deficit. Haec igitur venena ejus providens Deus, clausa licet ignoscentiae janua, et intinctionis sera obstructa, aliquid adhuc permisit patere. Collocavit in vestibulo poenitentiam secundam, quae pulsantibus patefaciat: sed jam semel, quia jam secundo. Sed amplius nunquam, quia proxime frustra. Non enim et hoc semel satis est? Habes, quod jam non merebaris; amisisti enim quod acceperas. Si tibi indulgentia Domini accommodat, unde restituas quod amiseras, iterato beneficio gratus esto, nedum ampliato: majus est enim restituere, quam dare: quoniam miserius est perdidisse, quam omnino non accepisse. Verum non statim succidendus ac subruendus est animus desperatione, si secundae quis poenitentiae debitor fuerit: pigeat sane peccare rursus, sed rursus poenitere non pigeat: pigeat iterum periclitari, sed non iterum liberari. Neminem pudeat; iteratae valetudinis iteranda medicina est: gratus in Dominum exstiteris, si quod tibi Dominus offert, non recusaveris: offendisti, sed reconciliari adhuc potes. Habes cui satisfacias, et quidem volentem.
pass_a_gloss: So far, Christ Lord, it happens that your servants speak or hear about the discipline of repentance, as long as it is not necessary for those hearing to sin: or they know nothing about repentance, they require nothing of it. It grieves to weave in the mention of a fertile, or rather now a last hope, lest by retracting the remaining help of repenting, we seem to demonstrate a space for still sinning. Let it be absent, that someone interprets it thus, as if for him even now a path to sinning is open, because a path to repenting is open; and the abundance of heavenly clemency makes an opportunity for human recklessness. No one is worse for this reason, because God is better, sinning as many times as he is forgiven. Nevertheless, he will certainly have an end to escaping, when he will not have an end to offending. We have escaped once; let us not henceforth bring ourselves into dangerous situations, and if we seem about to escape again. Many, having been freed from shipwreck, from then on renounce both the ship and the sea, and they honor God's benefit, their own salvation, with the memory of the danger. I praise fear, I love reverence, they do not want to be a burden to divine mercy again; they fear being seen to trample, what they have attained; they avoid experiencing again with good solicitude what they have once learned to fear. Thus, the measure of recklessness is a testimony of fear. And fear of man is honor to God. But indeed that most stubborn enemy never takes a rest from his malice. And yet he rages most, when he senses that a man is fully freed; then he is most inflamed, while being extinguished. He must grieve and groan, because forgiveness of sins is permitted, so many works of death in man are destroyed, so many titles of damnation are erased. He grieves because that sinner will judge him and his angels, a servant of Christ. And so he watches, he attacks, he besieges, if he can strike the eyes with carnal concupiscence, or entangle the soul with worldly allurements, or overturn faith with the fear of earthly power, or turn away from the certain path with perverse traditions: he does not lack scandals or temptations. Therefore, God, providing for these poisons of his, although the door of forgiveness is closed and the gate of baptism is obstructed, has still permitted something to be open. He has placed second repentance in the entrance hall, which opens to those knocking: but now only once, because now for the second time. But never more, because most recently in vain. Is this not enough even once? You have what you no longer deserved; for you lost what you had received. If the Lord's indulgence is accommodated to you, from which you can restore what you had lost, be grateful for the repeated benefit, not to mention the increased one: for it is greater to restore than to give, since it is more wretched to have lost than not to have received at all. But indeed the soul is not to be immediately cut down and overthrown with desperation, if someone is a debtor of second repentance: it is right to grieve to sin again, but not to grieve to repent again: it is right to grieve to be in danger again, but not to grieve to be freed again. Let no one be ashamed; repeated medicine is to be repeated for repeated sickness: you will be grateful to the Lord, if you do not refuse what the Lord offers to you: you have offended, but you can still be reconciled. You have one to whom you can make satisfaction, and indeed one who is willing.

choices.why: vice opposed to fear of God

pass_b_english: So far, Christ our Lord, it has happened that your servants speak or hear about the discipline of repentance only as long as those listening still feel no need to sin — or until they know nothing of repentance and require nothing of it. It grieves me to weave in the mention of a fertile hope, or rather a final one, lest by holding out this remaining help we seem to be granting a license to keep on sinning. God forbid anyone should twist this into thinking the path to sin stands open just because the path to repentance does, letting the abundance of heavenly mercy fuel human recklessness. No one should become worse on the grounds that God is better, sinning as often as he is forgiven. Even so, there will certainly be an end to escaping when there is no longer an end to offending. We have escaped once; let us not throw ourselves into danger again, even if we imagine we might escape a second time. Many who have been freed from shipwreck renounce both the ship and the sea afterward, honoring God's gift — their own salvation — by remembering the peril. I praise fear, I love reverence: they refuse to burden divine mercy again, they dread being seen to trample what they have gained, and with wholesome anxiety they avoid experiencing again what they once learned to fear. Thus the measure of recklessness becomes a testimony to fear, and fear of man is honor to God. But that most stubborn enemy never rests from his malice. Indeed he rages most fiercely when he senses a man fully freed; then he burns hottest while he is being extinguished. He must grieve and groan because forgiveness of sins is granted, so many works of death in man are demolished, so many titles of damnation erased. He grieves because that sinner — a servant of Christ — will judge him and his angels. So he watches, attacks, besieges, trying to strike the eyes with carnal lust, entangle the soul with worldly allurements, overturn faith with fear of earthly power, or drag a man from the sure path with perverse traditions; he never lacks scandals or temptations. Therefore God, foreseeing these poisons, has still left something open even though the door of forgiveness is shut and the gate of baptism barred. He has placed a second repentance in the vestibule, which opens for those who knock — but only once, because this is the second time. Never again, because the last time proved useless. Is not even this once enough? You have what you no longer deserved, since you lost what you had received. If the Lord's indulgence is extended to you so that you can restore what you lost, be grateful for the repeated gift, let alone an increased one; for it is greater to restore than to give, since it is more wretched to have lost than never to have received at all. Yet the soul must not be immediately cut down and overthrown by despair if someone owes a second repentance: it is right to grieve over sinning again, but not over repenting again; right to grieve over being in danger again, but not over being freed again. Let no one be ashamed: repeated sickness calls for repeated medicine. You will prove grateful to the Lord if you do not refuse what he offers: you have offended, but you can still be reconciled. You have one to whom you can make satisfaction — and one who is willing.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the complex conditional structures and the theological distinctions regarding 'second repentance'. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent, accurate English version that preserves all agency and modality. All clauses in the single paragraph were checked.
